tags.gist: Wants competency assessed as task-specific and consequence-sensitive, including uncertainty recognition, abstention, escalation and reliability after deployment, since fluency is not judgment.
Lists seven recommendations spanning risk factors, deployed-device testing, specialist comparators, team evaluation, independent adjudication, triggered reassessment and agentic boundaries.
Says the generalist-specialist distinction should shape risk when safety depends on whether the user can spot a specialty-specific error.
Illustrates with radiation oncology: a plausible recommendation can hide an unsafe fractionation or overlooked prior course visible only against full history.
Would weigh error detectability, reversibility and realistic specialist escalation for functions extending specialty knowledge to generalists; disclaimers are not safeguards.
Lists mitigations such as narrow intended use, provenance, calibrated uncertainty, abstention and workflow controls on high-consequence recommendations.
Wants benchmarking and clinical confirmation by qualified specialists where safe interpretation needs specialist knowledge, even for generalist users.
Calls the benchmarking structure a useful start if it tests the deployed configuration, and warns it is no proxy for clinical confirmation.
Would add consequence-graded failure modes, decision-boundary cases, abstention, traceability, multi-turn robustness and automation-bias testing to the elements.
Wants ceilings on critical errors and failures to abstain or escalate in acceptance criteria, regardless of strong overall performance.
Accepts sponsor-developed assets for specialized tasks if protocol and scoring are independently reviewed, with sequestered, rotating and external cases.
Wants a specialist panel to define the reference standard for specialty tasks; a median generalist should not set acceptable safety.
Proposes four evaluation conditions, device alone, user alone, user with device and a specialist panel, to separate device capability from team effects.
Would make team performance a principal basis where review is intended, keep device-alone testing, and credit oversight only when users demonstrably catch errors.
Wants prespecified acceptance criteria stratified by consequence that also cover omissions, unnecessary or delayed care, unjustified certainty and missed specialist referral.
Gives third parties roles in protocol review, benchmark governance, adjudication and disputed-error review for moderate and high-consequence functions.
Wants adjudicators matched to the function and setting, specialty-certified for specialty tasks, with independence criteria on finances and sponsor influence.
Wants third-party participation proportionate to risk, with reusable protocols and transparent standards so it does not become a barrier or a closed market.
Would pair periodic review with reassessment on triggers, since a fixed cadence misses changes to model, prompts, retrieval, guardrails or tools.
Lists triggers such as material changes, new settings, sentinel events, rising overrides and subgroup degradation, with sampling enriched for high-consequence outputs.
Wants monitoring to follow outcomes that matter clinically and process failures, including near misses, rather than lexical similarity or general accuracy.
Gives clinicians, institutions and societies reporting and local-monitoring roles while manufacturers keep responsibility for funding, operating and reporting.
Wants low-friction reporting that keeps clinical context, manufacturer summaries of changes and findings, and no diffusion of ownership of the response.
Says agentic systems need evaluation of the whole action chain because small early errors can compound into high-consequence actions.
Wants each agentic function to define an autonomy boundary, with hard human checkpoints for high-consequence or irreversible actions.
Wants premarket tests under tool failure, stale sources, prompt injection and nonresponse, with criteria on least privilege, audit logs and rollback.
Wants more frequent postmarket oversight when an agent can act, with reassessment triggered by changes to any component of the chain.
Says a supervisory model may help monitoring but cannot count as independent validation until its own performance and shared dependencies are evaluated.
Calls the competency approach promising provided competency is defined per task and tested where the output will be used, distinguishing fluency from judgment.
Wants evidence, adjudication, human-factors testing and monitoring to strengthen as a device directs action more and its errors are harder to detect.
